title_original: What Artists and Writers Are Thankful for This Year
excerpt_original: Shahzia Sikander, Christina Sharpe, Beatriz Cortez, and other members of our community share what and whom they’re grateful for after a year of both uncertainty and solidarity in the art world.

blocks.text: As every self-help book will tell you, it's important to practice gratitude, especially in the darkest times. Unraveling Thanksgiving's history as a tribute to Indigenous dispossession, this week is a time to do just that — give thanks for the support and solidarity that keeps us going. This year, we invited artists, writers, and art workers from our extended community to share what and whom they're thankful for. They shouted out their friends, students, favorite artworks, books, and more. Their contributions fill us with hope and faith in the future, and for that we're grateful.

Seeing Lorna Simpson’s “Wigs” in a study room with my students at the Museum of Modern Art is an experience in the auratic mysteries of the object: its ability to speak, mutely and persistently. Are we looking at an heirloom catalog or a series of specimens, evidence of female choice, or racial fetishization? The ethical dilemma underlying the very notion of collecting haunts museums themselves as institutional repositories of imperial and colonial appetite. Yet, given our current political moment when inconvenient histories are being systemically and institutionally erased, museums also provide spaces for critical remembrance, crucial holders of the past and how that past continues to shape our present. I remain grateful to those museums today who see education and critical analysis as integral parts of their mission.

blocks.caption: Students viewing Lorna Simpson’s “Wigs” (1994) at the Museum of Modern Art (courtesy Anne Cheng)

blocks.text: PS — Is it a coincidence that institutions are starving the humanities and the arts just when common human decency and the ideal of a common good are radically disintegrating? Art matters precisely for its ability to articulate and invoke the ineffable. Think these lines from William Carlos Williams:
It is difficult to get the news from poems yet men die miserably every day for lack of what is found there.
